title: At the café — and the noun as object
goal: Order drinks and food, and set up the first case: the accusative, the form a noun takes when it is the object of an action — and which, for half of all nouns, turns out not to change at all.
bekal: order and pay with polite, natural sentences
put nouns into the accusative, and know when they don't change
use the object pronouns *me, te, ga, je, nas, vas, ih*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — U kafani
dialogs.intro: A small café in Baščaršija, low wooden chairs outside. Budi and Amina sit down; the waiter comes over without waiting to be called.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Za mene čaj, molim. S limunom.
lines.id: Tea for me, please. With lemon.

notes: **Notice the ending *-u* turning up again and again:** *kafa → kafu*, *voda → vodu*, *pita → pitu*. That's the feminine accusative, and it's what makes your order sound right. *Jednu kafu, molim* is a sentence you'll say more often than any other in Bosnia.

**Adjectives change along with their noun.** *Bosanska kafa* becomes *bosansku kafu*; *jedna* becomes *jednu*. A noun never moves alone — the whole group in front of it moves too. That's why the adjective table at the back of this course has a row for each case.

***Za mene* — after a preposition, pronouns use the long form.** *Za mene, za tebe, za njega, bez nas.* The short forms (*me, te, ga*) never appear after a preposition, and never at the start of a sentence. This is part of the second-slot rule set up fully in unit 12.

***Molim* at the end of a sentence is the shortest way to be polite.** Fuller forms: *Molim vas* (to someone you address formally) or *Molim te* (to a friend). And *Izvolite!* from the waiter means "here you are, what can I get you" — you'll hear it every time you enter a shop, and it's also used when handing something to you.

**Pita.** Not Greek flatbread, but thin pastry rolled around a filling and baked in a coil — the most typical Bosnian home food. Its name depends on the filling: *burek* (meat — and only meat; calling any other kind *burek* will get you a friendly but firm correction), *sirnica* (cheese), *zeljanica* (spinach), *krompiruša* (potato). Ask *Imate li pitu?* almost anywhere and the answer will be *Imamo*.

grammars.title: Akuzativ — the object form, and half of it doesn't change
body: The first of seven cases, and deliberately this one first: it's the most used, and the cheapest to learn — because for half of all nouns the form is exactly the same as the dictionary form. English has a trace of the same idea: *he* sees, but someone sees *him*.
after: **You really only need to remember two rows:** feminine words ending in *-a* change it to **-u**, and **animate** masculine words add **-a**. Everything else doesn't move at all. If all you remember today is *kafa → kafu*, seventy percent of your orders are already right.

**"Animate" means people and animals.** *Vidim brata* (I see my brother), *Vidim konja* (I see a horse), but *Vidim grad* (I see the city — inanimate, no change). This rule applies only to **masculine singular** words; feminine and neuter don't care whether something is alive.

**The whole group in front of the noun changes too.** *Ovaj dobar sok* stays *ovaj dobar sok* (inanimate), but *ova dobra kafa* becomes *ovu dobru kafu*, and *ovaj dobar student* becomes *ovog dobrog studenta*. The full adjective table is in the grammar summary; for now, copy ready-made pairs: *jednu bosansku kafu*.

**The accusative also comes after some prepositions**, and the most important use is **destination**: *idem u grad* (into town), *idem na posao* (to work), *ovo je za tebe* (this is for you), *kroz park* (through the park). Compare *u gradu* and *na poslu* — that's the locative, the **location** form, set up in unit 9. One preposition, two cases, two meanings: *u grad* = into town, *u gradu* = in town.

grammars.title: Object pronouns — me, te, ga, je…
body: Just like nouns, pronouns have an object form (English does too: *I → me, he → him*). And like *sam* and *je*, they come in two shapes: short for everyday use, long for emphasis.

head: Person
Long
Short
Example
rows: *Čekaš li me?* — Are you waiting for me?
*Ja te čekam.* — I'm waiting for you.

after: **The short form sits in the second slot and never starts a sentence.** *Ja te čekam* — not *Te čekam*. If there's no other word in front, the order flips: *Čekam te.* This rule is exactly the same as for *sam, si, je* in unit 1, and the full version comes in unit 12.

**The long form is used in two situations**: after a preposition (*za mene, bez tebe, s njim*) and when you want emphasis (*Mene čekaš, ne njega?* — "it's *me* you're waiting for, not him?"). In ordinary conversation, the short form is what you use almost all the time.

***Je* or *ju* for "her"?** Both mean the same. *Ju* is used to avoid clashing with *je* from *biti*: *Vidio ju je* (he has seen her) sounds neater than *vidio je je*. Otherwise *je* is the usual one.

**The verbs that most often pair with these forms:** *čekati* (to wait for), *vidjeti* (to see), *zvati* (to call), *razumjeti* (to understand), *voljeti* (to love), *tražiti* (to look for), *poznavati* (to know a person). Practice three short sentences every day — *Čekam te. Vidim ga. Ne razumijem ih.* — and these little words will stop feeling foreign within a week.

blocks.text: The sequence is always the same, and barely changes anywhere in Bosnia: the waiter comes and says *Izvolite*, you name your order in the accusative with *molim*, and at the end you call out *Račun, molim!*

head: Bosanski
Say it
English
rows: What can I get you? (from the waiter)

blocks.title: Three things to know before you sit down
items: **Bosnian coffee is not espresso.** *Bosanska kafa* is ground very fine, boiled in a *džezva*, and served with its grounds. It's drunk without stirring, slowly, while nibbling a sugar cube. If you want Italian-style coffee, ask for it by name: *espreso*, *makijato*, *kapućino*.

**The price includes your seat for as long as you like.** Nobody will move you on; one coffee can last you two hours, and that's the custom. The waiter won't bring the bill until you ask — *Račun, molim!*
**Tipping: round up.** There's no fixed percentage. If the bill is 8.50 KM, handing over 10 KM and saying *Zadržite kusur* is more than enough.
